# Cassava

<!-- BEGIN: hmi-opening -->
<div class="hmi-quick-read">
  <div class="hmi-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>
  <p>Lead, cadmium, arsenic and other metals in cassava root, flour, gari and tapioca are reported as monitoring results, with processing, limits, testing and controls kept distinct.</p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Metals of concern:</strong> the metals named by the studies cited on this page.</li>
    <li><strong>Main drivers:</strong> form, origin and preparation stay separate.</li>
    <li><strong>Practical framing:</strong> this page does not pool those studies into one typical value.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

This page draws on evidence from [[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|WHO]], [[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|European Commission]], and [[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|Codex Alimentarius]], together with 13 peer-reviewed studies. The complete citation list is at the bottom of the page.
<!-- END: hmi-opening -->

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="cassava-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="cassava-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="cassava-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Lead is the metal to check in cassava: 18 of 50 European root results exceeded the 100 µg/kg limit, while roots from the Americas were far lower; cadmium, arsenic and mercury were mostly low.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Lead decides most cassava questions; mercury, lead and cadmium are highest in cassava from gold-mining districts.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">A. <a id="decision-summary"></a>
## Cassava overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Lead is the metal that decides most cassava questions. In WHO GEMS/Food, European cassava root results had a median of 46 µg/kg in random sampling and 92 µg/kg where sampling was not described, and 18 of 50 results exceeded 100 µg/kg, the EU and Codex maximum for root and tuber vegetables.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span were lower, with a median of 9 µg/kg and a maximum of 82 µg/kg across 26 roots.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cadmium, arsenic and mercury were mostly low or below detection in monitored cassava.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> No European cassava root result exceeded the EU cadmium limit of 50 µg/kg for tropical roots and tubers, and most total arsenic and mercury results were non-detects.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span <a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as cassava

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers cassava (Manihot esculenta) root and the foods made directly from it: raw, boiled, fried or roasted root and its peel, cassava flour including fermented lafun and amala flour, gari, fufu, and cassava starch sold as tapioca.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">A. Wolle · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/barber2025-baby-food-elements-us">Toxic elements in baby and young children&#39;s foods in the US and correlation to ingredients</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Additives &amp; Contaminants: Part B</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/barber2025-baby-food-elements-us">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Cyanide from cassava’s cyanogenic glycosides is a natural toxicant rather than a heavy metal, so it is outside this page even though the EU sets limits of 50 mg/kg for fresh peeled root and 10 mg/kg for cassava and tapioca flour.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Names need care. GEMS/Food includes results labelled only “Tapioca” or “tapioca, see cassava”, which may describe the root or the starch, so this page reports them as tapioca of unstated form.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Nigerian studies, amala and fufu are named dishes whose raw material and moisture state are not always stated.<sup class="cite">[[sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iyabo OO, Ogundiran MB, Adebayo OL · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Toxic and Essential Metals in Staple Foods Commonly Consumed by Students in Ekiti State, South West, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-cassava" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-cassava-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of cassava, group and metal. Raw root, cooked cassava, flour, gari, fufu and starch are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with fresh or as-sold results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results for the same form of cassava. Same-study contrasts compare a treated flour with its untreated control, or cooked dried with cooked fresh cassava. Held rows failed a check against their own paper and are shown but not compared.</p>

WHO regions are reporting regions, not growing areas. Many results are non-detects with differing limits, which widens the bounds. Akwatia farms (diamond-mining town, Eastern Region; farms along the Birim river); fresh roots purchased from farms on five occasions March-June 2019, washed and peeled. Fried in certified commercial oil (&#39;500 g sample: 1000 L oil&#39; as printed) in a stainless-steel pan on a hot plate set at 200 °C for 25 min; cooled and milled. Analysed by ICP-MS after microwave HNO3/H2O2 digestion of ~1 g as-prepared homogenate; total As (no speciation). <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach cassava

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Cassava takes up metals from the soil it grows in.<sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras P · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Trace elements in farmland soils and crops, and probabilistic health risk assessment in areas influenced by mining activity in Ecuador</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Geochemistry and Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In an orchard on gold-mining waste in Ponce Enríquez, Ecuador, where soils held 1.06–1.94 mg/kg cadmium and up to 422 mg/kg arsenic, the cassava root carried 60 µg/kg cadmium and 2,350 µg/kg nickel but arsenic and lead below 200 and 100 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras P · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Trace elements in farmland soils and crops, and probabilistic health risk assessment in areas influenced by mining activity in Ecuador</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Geochemistry and Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In the same orchards cassava was one of three crops with arsenic below detection and among the lowest in cadmium of nine crops, while lettuce reached 12,500 µg/kg arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras P · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Trace elements in farmland soils and crops, and probabilistic health risk assessment in areas influenced by mining activity in Ecuador</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Geochemistry and Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Most of the lead found in monitoring is likely surface or soil-related contamination of the root or post-harvest contact rather than a property of the plant, but no source in the ledger tested that directly. The EU limit for root and tuber vegetables applies after washing and separating the edible part, which shows where regulators expect soil to be removed.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A Nigerian lafun survey attributes its low cadmium to reduced use of cadmium-containing fertilisers, without data on fertiliser use.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EDITED BY Arun K. Bhunia, Purdue University, United States REVIEWED BY Marco E. Mng&#39;ong&#39;o, sold in selected markets—taken Mbeya University of Science, Technology · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide">OPEN ACCESS potential toxic levels of cyanide</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Gold mining is the clearest source in the evidence. Near goldmines at Bogoso and Prestea in Ghana, peeled cassava flesh carried 122–168 µg/kg mercury at sites 1.5 to 14 km from the mines, with no clear fall-off with distance.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">A. Adjorlolo-Gasokpoh, A. A. Golow, J. Kambo-Dorsa · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana">Mercury in the Surface Soil and Cassava, Manihot esculenta (Flesh, Leaves and Peel) Near Goldmines at Bogoso and Prestea, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bull Environ Contam Toxicol</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In the Kade mining area, raw cassava held 301–426 µg/kg mercury and 24–30 µg/kg cadmium on a dry-weight basis, and peeled roots bought in the mining towns of Obuasi and Akwatia averaged 2,110 µg/kg lead and 120–160 µg/kg mercury, on a basis the paper does not state.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Cecilia Owusu-Agyemang Fobi, Guy Eshun, Twumasi Ankrah Kwarteng, Afia Sakyiwaa Amponsah, Prince Owusu Adoma · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana">Effect of Boiling on Heavy Metal and Cyanide Concentrations and Associated Health Risks in Cassava and Cocoyam From a Gold Mining Area in Kade, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Around Tarkwa’s gold mines, 33 cassava roots from 11 farming communities had a geometric mean of 180 µg/kg lead, with about 30% at 370–450 µg/kg, but only 4 µg/kg mercury; the paper labels its results as both wet and dry weight, so the basis is unresolved.<sup class="cite">[[sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bortey-Sam N, Nakayama SMM, Akoto O, Ikenaka Y, Fobil JN, Baidoo E, Mizukawa H, Ishizuka M · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Metalloid in Foodstuffs from Agricultural Soils around Tarkwa Area in Ghana, and Associated Human Health Risks</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2015)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/borteysam2015-tarkwa-cassava-plantain-soil-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Mercury sat in the edible flesh as well as the peel: at all four Ghanaian sites the outer skin held less mercury than the flesh beneath it, and the inner cortex held less at three.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">A. Adjorlolo-Gasokpoh, A. A. Golow, J. Kambo-Dorsa · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana">Mercury in the Surface Soil and Cassava, Manihot esculenta (Flesh, Leaves and Peel) Near Goldmines at Bogoso and Prestea, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bull Environ Contam Toxicol</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Processing water is another route. When peeled roots were soaked for flour, the soaking water itself gained lead, cadmium and chromium, showing that metals move between the root and the water in both directions depending on its quality.<sup class="cite">[[sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Albishi TS, Adaigho D, Alqahtani NK, Sami R, Uguru H, Helal M, Alaoufi SH, Alkaltham MS, Osiga-Aibangbee D, Okolotu GI, Emumejaye EP, Qari SH · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">In vitro evaluation of bio-fortification effects on the nutritional quality, toxicological safety, and antioxidant of cassava (Manihot esculenta) flour, and environmental safety of processing water, using natural additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which forms and markets measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

For lead in raw cassava root, the lowest results in the evidence are those submitted to GEMS/Food from the Americas: a median of 9 µg/kg across 26 imported roots in 2014–2016, with a maximum of 82 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European submissions were higher, with medians of 46 µg/kg under random sampling and 92 µg/kg where sampling was not described.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO regions are reporting regions, not growing areas, so this is a lowest observed pattern by market, not a ranking of producing countries.

Within Europe, lead fell over time and differed by origin label.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> 17 of 39 root results from 2008–2012 exceeded 100 µg/kg against 1 of 11 from 2013–2019, and roots labelled imported had a median of 140 µg/kg against 64 µg/kg for those labelled domestic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are national monitoring submissions, not a fixed panel of suppliers, and the export does not name the country of growth.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Among processed forms, cassava starch and flour submitted from the Americas were lowest for lead, at a median of 10 µg/kg (15 starch and 3 flour results).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Results labelled “Tapioca” in Europe were among the highest, with a median of 115 µg/kg and 12 of 22 above 100 µg/kg, but their form is not stated.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Nigeria, market lafun ranged from 28 to 53 µg/kg lead across five towns, while single vendor samples of amala flour, fufu and garri reported 140, 150 and 300 µg/kg, and cassava from around Owerri 330 µg/kg lead and 100 µg/kg cadmium, all on an unstated basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EDITED BY Arun K. Bhunia, Purdue University, United States REVIEWED BY Marco E. Mng&#39;ong&#39;o, sold in selected markets—taken Mbeya University of Science, Technology · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide">OPEN ACCESS potential toxic levels of cyanide</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bhunia2023-open-access-potential-toxic-levels-of-cyanide">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-form-of-cassava-measured-lowest-in-lead" data-anchor="which-form-of-cassava-measured-lowest-in-lead" data-question="Which form of cassava measured lowest in lead?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which form of cassava measured lowest in lead?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Starch and flour submitted to GEMS/Food from the Americas were lowest, at a median of 10 µg/kg, followed by raw root from the same region at 9 µg/kg median.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European “tapioca” of unstated form and European root were higher, and Nigerian vendor samples of garri, fufu and amala reported 140–300 µg/kg on an unstated basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iyabo OO, Ogundiran MB, Adebayo OL · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Toxic and Essential Metals in Staple Foods Commonly Consumed by Students in Ekiti State, South West, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/iyabo2015-ekiti-staple-foods-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These forms come from different markets and laboratories, so the pattern is a lowest observed comparison, not a ranking of processing methods.

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-imported-cassava-higher-in-lead-than-locally-grown-cassava" data-anchor="is-imported-cassava-higher-in-lead-than-locally-grown-cassava" data-question="Is imported cassava higher in lead than locally grown cassava?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is imported cassava higher in lead than locally grown cassava?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In European GEMS/Food submissions, roots labelled imported had a median of 140 µg/kg lead against 64 µg/kg for those labelled domestic, and 12 of 21 imported roots exceeded 100 µg/kg against 6 of 28 domestic ones.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The export does not name the country of growth, so this cannot identify which producing countries are higher.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Soaking, drying and cooking

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Two kinds of processing evidence exist, and neither is large. In a laboratory experiment with one cultivar from one farm, soaking peeled roots in tap water for 48 hours before drying and milling gave flour about 11% lower in lead (61 against 69 µg/kg dry weight), 8% lower in cadmium and 4% lower in chromium than unsoaked roots.<sup class="cite">[[sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Albishi TS, Adaigho D, Alqahtani NK, Sami R, Uguru H, Helal M, Alaoufi SH, Alkaltham MS, Osiga-Aibangbee D, Okolotu GI, Emumejaye EP, Qari SH · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">In vitro evaluation of bio-fortification effects on the nutritional quality, toxicological safety, and antioxidant of cassava (Manihot esculenta) flour, and environmental safety of processing water, using natural additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Soaking in plant-extract solutions with 1% plant powder added to the flour gave larger reductions, down to 21 µg/kg lead and 27 µg/kg cadmium, but the extracts and powders were never tested for metals and the results are repeat analyses of a single lot per treatment.<sup class="cite">[[sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Albishi TS, Adaigho D, Alqahtani NK, Sami R, Uguru H, Helal M, Alaoufi SH, Alkaltham MS, Osiga-Aibangbee D, Okolotu GI, Emumejaye EP, Qari SH · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">In vitro evaluation of bio-fortification effects on the nutritional quality, toxicological safety, and antioxidant of cassava (Manihot esculenta) flour, and environmental safety of processing water, using natural additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cooking lowered lead and mercury per kilogram in the one study that measured the same roots before and after.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In two Ghanaian mining towns, peeled cassava averaged 2,110 µg/kg lead; boiling for 30 minutes gave 600–610 µg/kg, frying 70–80 µg/kg and roasting 100 µg/kg in Akwatia, while mercury fell from 120–160 to 50–60 µg/kg when boiled and 20–30 µg/kg when fried, and fell least when roasted (110 µg/kg in both towns).<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The results were not corrected for water lost or gained or oil taken up during cooking, and heat does not destroy metals, so part of the drop may reflect transfer to cooking water or dilution rather than removal.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

A second Ghanaian study reports large reductions in mercury and cadmium after boiling, but it measured raw cassava on a dry-weight basis and does not state the basis for boiled cassava, so its raw-to-boiled differences cannot be read as a cooking effect.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Cecilia Owusu-Agyemang Fobi, Guy Eshun, Twumasi Ankrah Kwarteng, Afia Sakyiwaa Amponsah, Prince Owusu Adoma · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana">Effect of Boiling on Heavy Metal and Cyanide Concentrations and Associated Health Risks in Cassava and Cocoyam From a Gold Mining Area in Kade, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food Science</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fobi2025-boiling-cassava-cocoyam-kade-ghana">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> African total diet monitoring adds that cooked dried cassava had a median of 82 µg/kg lead against 35 µg/kg for cooked fresh cassava in 2018 submissions; these are different foods sampled as eaten.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-soaking-cassava-remove-heavy-metals" data-anchor="does-soaking-cassava-remove-heavy-metals" data-question="Does soaking cassava remove heavy metals?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does soaking cassava remove heavy metals?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only partly, and the evidence is one laboratory experiment. Soaking peeled roots in tap water for 48 hours lowered flour lead by about 11% and cadmium by 8%, and the metals appeared in the soaking water.<sup class="cite">[[sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Albishi TS, Adaigho D, Alqahtani NK, Sami R, Uguru H, Helal M, Alaoufi SH, Alkaltham MS, Osiga-Aibangbee D, Okolotu GI, Emumejaye EP, Qari SH · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">In vitro evaluation of bio-fortification effects on the nutritional quality, toxicological safety, and antioxidant of cassava (Manihot esculenta) flour, and environmental safety of processing water, using natural additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> No study measured the traditional long fermentation used for fufu or lafun against unfermented flour.

</div>
</details>

<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation from field to flour

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Controls for metals in cassava act at the field, during flour processing and at lot release. The only measured processing comparison is laboratory soaking, which lowered lead by about a tenth in water alone; the larger plant-extract effects come from one experiment without a check on the added materials.<sup class="cite">[[sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Albishi TS, Adaigho D, Alqahtani NK, Sami R, Uguru H, Helal M, Alaoufi SH, Alkaltham MS, Osiga-Aibangbee D, Okolotu GI, Emumejaye EP, Qari SH · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">In vitro evaluation of bio-fortification effects on the nutritional quality, toxicological safety, and antioxidant of cassava (Manihot esculenta) flour, and environmental safety of processing water, using natural additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/albishi2026-cassava-flour-biofortification">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Field evidence is observational: cassava from a mining-waste orchard stayed below detection for lead and arsenic but exceeded the EU cadmium limit for tropical roots.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras P · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Trace elements in farmland soils and crops, and probabilistic health risk assessment in areas influenced by mining activity in Ecuador</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Geochemistry and Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Boiling or frying peeled roots lowered lead and mercury per kilogram in one laboratory comparison from Ghanaian mining towns, but peeling did not remove mercury, which was present in the flesh.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjorlologasokpoh2012-mercury-cassava-goldmines-ghana|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">A. Cooking changes the food as well as its metal content. Frying gave the lowest lead and mercury per kilogram in the Ghanaian comparison, but it adds oil and removes water in ways the study did not measure, and boiling moves metals into water that is then discarded.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adjei-Mensah R, Ofori H, Tortoe C, Johnson PT, Aryee D, Frimpong SK · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Effect of home processing methods on the levels of heavy metal contaminants in four food crops grown in and around two mining towns in Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 8 (2021) 1830–1838</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adjeimensah2021-ghana-mining-home-processing-crops">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Choosing a crop for contaminated land involves trade-offs between metals. In the Ecuadorian mining area cassava was one of three crops with arsenic below detection but carried more nickel than most of the nine crops and cadmium above the EU tropical-root limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/romero-crespo2023-trace-elements-crops-ecuador-mining|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Romero-Crespo P, Jiménez-Oyola S, Salgado-Almeida B, Zambrano-Anchundia J, Goyburo-Chávez C, González-Valoys A, Higueras ## Exposure from cassava

Cassava is a staple in much of Africa, Latin America and Asia, so intake can be large where it is eaten daily, but no source in the ledger estimated lead or cadmium exposure from cassava with verified concentrations. A Colombian study reported a cadmium hazard quotient of 1.32 for cassava in one municipality, but the quotient cannot be reproduced from the reference dose the paper states and its concentrations are only in a supplement that is not in the library.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2023-health-risk-assessment-for-human-exposure-to-heavy|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span
